title: 7 Plane Accidents That Changed How We Fly

chapters.name: Intro
sentences: Flying is the safest way to travel. But it did not start out that way.
Almost every rule in aviation was written after something went terribly wrong.
Here are seven accidents that changed how we fly, and the rules each one left behind.
Rules that protect you every time you board a plane.
We start in 1956, in the sky above the Grand Canyon.

chapters.name: 1956 · Grand Canyon
sentences: On June thirtieth, 1956, two airliners took off from Los Angeles, three minutes apart.
One was a Super Constellation heading for Kansas City. The other was a D C seven heading for Chicago.
Together they carried one hundred and twenty-eight people.
Back then, once a plane left the main airways, nobody was watching it. Radar did not cover most of the sky.
Pilots were expected to look out of the window and avoid each other. The idea was called, see and be seen.
Both planes were cruising at twenty-one thousand feet, in an area of tall storm clouds.
At ten thirty-two in the morning, above the Grand Canyon, they collided.
Nobody survived. It was the deadliest airline disaster America had ever seen.
The public was shocked to learn that nobody had been controlling that part of the sky.
The next year, money was approved for radar, and for many more air traffic controllers.
And in 1958, a new law created the Federal Aviation Agency, known today as the F A A, with authority over all American airspace.
Lesson one. Someone must always be watching the sky.

chapters.name: 1973 · Fire Near Paris
sentences: Our second story takes place in July 1973.
A Boeing seven oh seven was flying from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, with one hundred and thirty-four people on board.
In those days, passengers smoked freely on planes.
As the jet descended toward Paris, a fire broke out in a rear toilet.
Investigators believe a lit cigarette had been thrown into the waste bin.
Thick smoke moved forward through the cabin, faster than the plane could come down.
The pilots landed in a field, about five kilometers short of the runway.
But for most people on board, it was already too late. One hundred and twenty-three died, most of them from the smoke.
That same year, smoking was banned in aircraft toilets in the United States.
And here is a detail you can check on your next flight.
Planes must still have an ashtray by the toilet door, in case someone breaks the rule. A bin full of paper is the worst place for a cigarette.
Lesson two. Smoke kills faster than fire.

chapters.name: 1977 · Tenerife
sentences: Story three is the deadliest accident in aviation history.
March twenty-seventh, 1977. A bomb at the main airport in the Canary Islands forced many flights to land at a small airport on Tenerife.
It had a single runway. And then, thick fog rolled in.
Two fully loaded jumbo jets were on that runway at the same time.
One was still taxiing along it. The other was at the far end, ready to leave.
The pilots could not see each other. The tower could see neither of them.
The waiting crew began its takeoff without a clearance.
The tower said to stand by. The other jet radioed that it was still on the runway.
But the two messages were sent at the same moment. In the cockpit, they arrived as a squeal.
The jets collided. Five hundred and eighty-three people died. Sixty-one survived.
Afterward, the language of flying was rewritten.
The word takeoff is now spoken only when a plane is truly cleared to go. Before that, pilots say departure.
Crews read important instructions back. And junior pilots are trained to speak up when something feels wrong.
Lesson three. Clear words save lives.

chapters.name: 1983 · Fire in the Cabin
sentences: Story four. June second, 1983.
A D C nine was flying north from Dallas, with forty-six people on board.
A fire started in or near the rear toilet. It burned out of sight, behind the cabin walls.
Investigators never found the exact cause.
The crew made an emergency landing at Cincinnati, and the doors were opened.
But the cabin was full of thick black smoke. People could not see the exits.
Less than ninety seconds after touchdown, fresh air fed the fire, and the cabin burst into flames.
Twenty-three of the forty-six people did not get out.
This accident changed the cabin you sit in today.
Smoke detectors became standard in aircraft toilets. Seat cushions were made to resist fire.
Lights were added along the floor, to lead you to an exit when smoke hides everything above.
And aircraft makers must show that a full plane can be emptied in ninety seconds.
Lesson four. In a fire, every second counts.

chapters.name: 1985 · The Microburst
sentences: Story five. August second, 1985, at Dallas Fort Worth airport.
A wide-body jet was coming in to land, with one hundred and sixty-three people on board.
Near the runway stood a thunderstorm. The crew decided to fly through it.
Hidden inside was a microburst. A column of air that drops out of a storm, hits the ground, and spreads out in every direction.
First it gives a plane a strong headwind. Seconds later, a powerful tailwind, and a push toward the ground.
The jet lost speed and height. It hit the ground more than a mile short of the runway.
It struck a car on a highway, and then two water tanks.
One hundred and thirty-seven people died, including the driver of the car.
At the time, pilots had no good way to see a microburst coming.
NASA went on to test radar that can spot wind shear ahead of a plane.
The F A A then required airliners to carry wind shear warning systems, and pilots began training to escape a microburst.
Lesson five. You cannot fight weather you cannot see.

chapters.name: 1988 · The Missing Roof
sentences: Story six. April twenty-eighth, 1988, in Hawaii.
A Boeing seven three seven was on a short island flight, with ninety-five people on board.
The plane was nineteen years old. It had made almost ninety thousand flights, most of them short hops in warm, salty air.
At twenty-four thousand feet, a section of the roof suddenly tore away.
About eighteen feet of the cabin was open to the sky.
One flight attendant was swept out of the aircraft. She was the only person who died.
The passengers were held in by their seat belts. Thirteen minutes later, the pilots landed on the island of Maui.
The cause was metal fatigue, made worse by corrosion. Thousands of flights had slowly weakened the joints in the plane's skin.
The airline's inspections had not caught the damage.
In 1991, a new American law told the F A A to write special rules for aging aircraft.
Older planes now get extra structural inspections, looking for tiny cracks before they can grow.
Lesson six. Metal gets tired too.

chapters.name: 2009 · A Winter Night
sentences: Our last story is from February 2009.
A small airliner was flying from Newark to Buffalo, New York, on a winter night.
On approach, the plane slowed down too much, and a stall warning shook the controls.
The right response is to lower the nose and add full power.
The captain pulled the nose up instead. The plane stalled, and fell onto a house.
All forty-nine people on board died, and one person on the ground.
Investigators found that both pilots were tired, although they could not say how much it mattered.
In 2010, a new American airline safety law followed.
First officers used to need only two hundred and fifty flight hours. Now, in most cases, they need fifteen hundred.
The rules on pilot rest were rewritten too.
Lesson seven. The pilot is part of the machine.

chapters.name: The Lessons
sentences: Seven accidents. Seven rules.
Radar that watches the sky. No smoking. Clear words on the radio.
Lights on the floor. Wind shear warnings. Checks for tired metal. And rested, experienced pilots.
Every one of these rules was paid for by people who never came home.
That is why flying keeps getting safer. Each lesson is learned once, and then shared with the whole world.
So next time the cabin lights dim, or a pilot repeats an instruction, you will know there is a story behind it.
